subject: maths
title: Year 5 Comparing and Ordering Fractions
seo_title: Year 5 Comparing Fractions Worksheets: Related Denominators, Mixed Numerals and Number Lines (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Compare and order fractions with the same and related denominators including mixed numerals, applying knowledge of factors and multiples; represent these fractions on a number line
meta_desc: Free Year 5 maths worksheets on comparing and ordering fractions for the Australian Curriculum (AC9M5N03): equivalent fractions with related denominators, fraction walls, improper fractions, mixed numerals, number lines and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, ideal for NAPLAN practice.
key_big: To compare fractions, make the denominators the same, then compare the numerators.
key_sub: 3/4 = 6/8, so 5/8 < 3/4. A bigger denominator means smaller parts: 1/8 < 1/4. 2 3/5 = 13/5, because 2 × 5 + 3 = 13.
body_html:
Same denominator

When the denominators are the same, the parts are the same size. Compare the numerators. For example, 58 > 38, because 5 eighths is more than 3 eighths.

When the numerators are the same, look at the size of the parts. 13 > 16, because thirds are bigger than sixths.

Related denominators

Denominators are related when one is a multiple of the other, like 4 and 8. Change one fraction into an equivalent fraction: multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number. Then compare the numerators.

Example

Which is greater: 58 or 34?

8 is a multiple of 4. 4 × 2 = 8, so 34 = 68. 6 eighths > 5 eighths.

Answer: 34

Improper fractions and mixed numerals

An improper fraction such as 114 is greater than 1. A mixed numeral such as 2 34 shows the same amount as wholes and a fraction.

Example

Write 2 35 as an improper fraction.

2 wholes = 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add 3 fifths: 10 + 3 = 13.

Answer: 135

Fractions on a number line

Split each whole into equal parts. Count the marks from 0. Numbers further to the right are greater.

Example

Order 54, 1 12 and 1 38 from smallest to largest.

Write them all in eighths: 54 = 108, 1 12 = 128, 1 38 = 118.

Answer: 54, 1 38, 1 12

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction: 18 > 14A bigger denominator means smaller parts: 18 < 14
Comparing only the numerators: 58 > 34 because 5 > 3Make the denominators the same first: 34 = 68, so 58 < 34
Multiplying only the numerator: 34 = 64Multiply both: 34 = 68
2 35 = 65 or 235Wholes × denominator, then add the numerator: 2 × 5 + 3 = 13, so 135

faq.q: What do Year 5 students learn about comparing fractions?
faq.a: In the Australian Curriculum (AC9M5N03), Year 5 students compare and order fractions with the same and related denominators, including mixed numerals, and show them on a number line. Related denominators are ones like 4 and 8, where one is a multiple of the other.

faq.q: How do you compare fractions with different denominators?
faq.a: If one denominator is a multiple of the other, change one fraction so both have the same denominator, then compare the numerators. For 5/8 and 3/4, 3/4 = 6/8, so 3/4 is greater.
A mixed numeral is a whole number and a fraction written together, such as 2 3/4. It shows the same amount as the improper fraction 11/4, because 2 × 4 + 3 = 11.

faq.q: Are comparing fractions questions on the Year 5 NAPLAN numeracy test?
faq.a: Fractions are part of the Number strand that NAPLAN numeracy draws on, so Year 5 students may meet questions on ordering fractions or placing them on a number line. Practising with fraction walls and number lines helps.

items.e: The bottom bar has 8 equal parts, so each half of the top bar is split into 4 parts. 1 half becomes 1 × 4 = 4 eighths. So 12 = 48.

items.e: The bottom bar has 8 equal parts, so each quarter of the top bar is split into 2 parts. 3 quarters become 3 × 2 = 6 eighths. So 34 = 68.

items.e: The bottom bar has 10 equal parts, so each fifth of the top bar is split into 2 parts. 2 fifths become 2 × 2 = 4 tenths. So 25 = 410.

items.e: The bottom bar has 12 equal parts, so each third of the top bar is split into 4 parts. 2 thirds become 2 × 4 = 8 twelfths. So 23 = 812.

34 = ?12
items.e: The bottom bar has 12 equal parts, so each quarter of the top bar is split into 3 parts. 3 quarters become 3 × 3 = 9 twelfths. So 34 = 912.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 12 is shaded. How many eighths are equal to 12?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each half is the same as 4 eighths, so 1 half lines up with 1 × 4 = 4 eighths. So 12 = 48.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 23 is shaded. How many twelfths are equal to 23?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each third is the same as 4 twelfths, so 2 thirds line up with 2 × 4 = 8 twelfths. So 23 = 812.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 35 is shaded. How many tenths are equal to 35?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each fifth is the same as 2 tenths, so 3 fifths line up with 3 × 2 = 6 tenths. So 35 = 610.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 34 is shaded. How many eighths are equal to 34?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each quarter is the same as 2 eighths, so 3 quarters line up with 3 × 2 = 6 eighths. So 34 = 68.

items.q: 56 = ?12
items.e: Look at the denominators: 6 × 2 = 12. Multiply the numerator by 2 too: 5 × 2 = 10. So 56 = 1012.

items.q: 38 = ?16
items.e: Look at the denominators: 8 × 2 = 16. Multiply the numerator by 2 too: 3 × 2 = 6. So 38 = 616.

items.q: 45 = ?20
items.e: Look at the denominators: 5 × 4 = 20. Multiply the numerator by 4 too: 4 × 4 = 16. So 45 = 1620.

items.q: 23 = ?9
items.e: Look at the denominators: 3 × 3 = 9. Multiply the numerator by 3 too: 2 × 3 = 6. So 23 = 69.

items.q: 34 = 9?
items.e: Look at the numerators: 3 × 3 = 9. Multiply the denominator by 3 too: 4 × 3 = 12. So 34 = 912.

items.q: 25 = 6?
items.e: Look at the numerators: 2 × 3 = 6. Multiply the denominator by 3 too: 5 × 3 = 15. So 25 = 615.

items.q: 56 = 10?
items.e: Look at the numerators: 5 × 2 = 10. Multiply the denominator by 2 too: 6 × 2 = 12. So 56 = 1012.

items.q: 68 = ?4
items.e: 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so divide the numerator by 2 too: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. So 68 = 34. Taking 4 away from the top and the bottom (to get 24) changes the value.

items.q: 1012 = ?6
items.e: 12 ÷ 2 = 6, so divide the numerator by 2 too: 10 ÷ 2 = 5. So 1012 = 56. Taking 6 away from the top and the bottom (to get 46) changes the value.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to 23?
items.e: 3 × 4 = 12, so multiply the numerator by 4 too: 2 × 4 = 8. So 23 = 812. 83 only multiplies the numerator, and 45 adds 2 to both numbers.

items.q: Which fraction is not equivalent to 34?
items.e: 56 is not equal to 34: 2 was added to the numerator and the denominator. Adding changes the value. The others are equivalent, because both numbers were multiplied by the same number (× 2, × 3, × 5).

sets.title: Compare fractions with the same and related denominators

items.q: Which is greater: 58 or 38?
items.e: The denominators are the same, so compare the numerators: 5 > 3. So 58 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 47 or 67?
items.e: The denominators are the same, so compare the numerators: 6 > 4. So 67 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 712 or 912?
items.e: The denominators are the same, so compare the numerators: 9 > 7. So 912 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 16 or 13?
items.e: The numerators are the same. Thirds are bigger parts than sixths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 13 is greater. The bigger denominator does not make the bigger fraction.

items.q: Which is greater: 110 or 15?
items.e: The numerators are the same. Fifths are bigger parts than tenths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 15 is greater. The bigger denominator does not make the bigger fraction.

items.q: Which is greater: 35 or 310?
items.e: The numerators are the same. Fifths are bigger parts than tenths, because the whole is cut into fewer parts. So 35 is greater. The bigger denominator does not make the bigger fraction.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Which is greater: 58 or 34?
items.e: 8 is a multiple of 4, so use eighths: 58 and 34 = 68. 6 > 5, so 34 is greater.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Which is greater: 23 or 712?
items.e: 12 is a multiple of 3, so use twelfths: 23 = 812 and 712. 8 > 7, so 23 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 35 or 710?
items.e: 10 is a multiple of 5, so use tenths: 35 = 610 and 710. 7 > 6, so 710 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 49 or 13?
items.e: 9 is a multiple of 3, so use ninths: 49 and 13 = 39. 4 > 3, so 49 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 56 or 1112?
items.e: 12 is a multiple of 6, so use twelfths: 56 = 1012 and 1112. 11 > 10, so 1112 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 34 or 68?
items.e: 8 is a multiple of 4, so use eighths: 34 = 68 and 68. The numerators are the same, so they are equal.

items.q: Which is greater: 12 or 512?
items.e: 12 is a multiple of 2, so use twelfths: 12 = 612 and 512. 6 > 5, so 12 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 710 or 1320?
items.e: 20 is a multiple of 10, so use twentieths: 710 = 1420 and 1320. 14 > 13, so 710 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 23 or 59?
items.e: 9 is a multiple of 3, so use ninths: 23 = 69 and 59. 6 > 5, so 23 is greater.

items.q:
Which sign goes in the box?
56 □ 1112
items.e: Use twelfths: 56 = 1012 and 1112. So 56 < 1112. The open side of the sign faces the greater fraction.

items.q:
Which sign goes in the box?
34 □ 912
items.e: Use twelfths: 34 = 912 and 912. So 34 = 912.

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: 310 > 25
712 > 34
56 < 23
38 < 12
items.e: Make the denominators the same. 12 = 48, so 38 < 48 is true. The others are false: 56 = 1012 > 812, 310 < 25 = 410 and 712 < 34 = 912.

items.q: Which is greater: 2 14 or 2 38?
items.e: Both have 2 wholes, so compare the fractions. 14 = 28, and 3 eighths > 2 eighths. So 2 38 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 2 12 or 94?
items.e: Write both in quarters: 2 12 = 104 (2 × 4 + 2 = 10), and 94 is 9 quarters. 10 > 9, so 2 12 is greater.

items.q: Each bar is 1 whole. 114 are shaded. Write this as a mixed numeral.
items.e: Each bar is 1 whole. 2 bars are full and 3 more parts are shaded in the last bar. So 114 = 2 34.

items.q: Each bar is 1 whole. 83 are shaded. Write this as a mixed numeral.
items.e: Each bar is 1 whole. 2 bars are full and 2 more parts are shaded in the last bar. So 83 = 2 23.

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed numeral.
items.e: Each whole is split into 3 equal parts, so each mark is 13. The arrow is 2 marks after 1. So it shows 1 23 = 53.

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed numeral.
items.e: Each whole is split into 4 equal parts, so each mark is 14. The arrow is 1 mark after 2. So it shows 2 14 = 94.

items.q: Write 72 as a mixed numeral.
items.e: How many 2s go into 7? 3 × 2 = 6, so there are 3 wholes. 7 − 6 = 1 is left over. So 72 = 3 12.

items.q: Write 135 as a mixed numeral.
items.e: How many 5s go into 13? 2 × 5 = 10, so there are 2 wholes. 13 − 10 = 3 are left over. So 135 = 2 35.

items.q: Write 174 as a mixed numeral.
items.e: How many 4s go into 17? 4 × 4 = 16, so there are 4 wholes. 17 − 16 = 1 is left over. So 174 = 4 14.

items.q: Write 196 as a mixed numeral.
items.e: How many 6s go into 19? 3 × 6 = 18, so there are 3 wholes. 19 − 18 = 1 is left over. So 196 = 3 16.

items.q: Write 2310 as a mixed numeral.
items.e: How many 10s go into 23? 2 × 10 = 20, so there are 2 wholes. 23 − 20 = 3 are left over. So 2310 = 2 310.

items.q: Write 298 as a mixed numeral.
items.e: How many 8s go into 29? 3 × 8 = 24, so there are 3 wholes. 29 − 24 = 5 are left over. So 298 = 3 58.

items.q: Write 227 as a mixed numeral.
items.e: How many 7s go into 22? 3 × 7 = 21, so there are 3 wholes. 22 − 21 = 1 is left over. So 227 = 3 17.

items.q: Write 2 35 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 55, so 2 wholes are 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add the 3: 10 + 3 = 13. So 2 35 = 135.

items.q: Write 1 23 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 33, so 1 whole is 1 × 3 = 3 thirds. Add the 2: 3 + 2 = 5. So 1 23 = 53.

items.q: Write 3 14 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 44, so 3 wholes are 3 × 4 = 12 quarters. Add the 1: 12 + 1 = 13. So 3 14 = 134.

items.q: Write 4 23 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 33, so 4 wholes are 4 × 3 = 12 thirds. Add the 2: 12 + 2 = 14. So 4 23 = 143.

items.q: Write 1 710 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 1010, so 1 whole is 1 × 10 = 10 tenths. Add the 7: 10 + 7 = 17. So 1 710 = 1710.

items.q: Write 5 38 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 88, so 5 wholes are 5 × 8 = 40 eighths. Add the 3: 40 + 3 = 43. So 5 38 = 438.

items.q: Write 2 56 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 66, so 2 wholes are 2 × 6 = 12 sixths. Add the 5: 12 + 5 = 17. So 2 56 = 176.

items.q: Which improper fraction is greater than 3?
items.e: 3 wholes = 3 × 4 = 12 quarters. 134 is 1 quarter more, so 134 = 3 14 is greater than 3. 124 is exactly 3, and 114 is less than 3.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to 3 wholes?
items.e: Each whole is 55, so 3 wholes = 3 × 5 = 155. 35 is less than 1, and 85 comes from adding 3 + 5.

sets.title: Order fractions and mixed numerals on a number line

items.q: Which fraction is the greatest?
items.e: Write them all in sixteenths: 34 = 1216, 58 = 1016, 1116, 12 = 816. The greatest is 1216, so the answer is 34.

items.q: Which fraction is the smallest?
items.e: Write them all in twelfths: 23 = 812, 56 = 1012, 712, 512. The smallest is 512, so the answer is 512.

items.q: Which fraction is the greatest?
items.e: Write them all in twentieths: 35 = 1220, 710 = 1420, 1320, 25 = 820. The greatest is 1420, so the answer is 710.

items.q: Which number is the greatest?
items.e: Write them all in eighths: 1 34 = 148, 158, 1 12 = 128, 138. The greatest is 158, so the answer is 158.

items.q: Which letter shows 74?
items.e: Each whole is split into 4 equal parts, so each mark is 14. 74 = 1 34: go to 1, then 3 more marks. That is letter D.

items.q: Which letter shows 1 13?
items.e: Each whole is split into 3 equal parts, so each mark is 13. 1 13 = 43: go to 1, then 1 more mark. That is letter C.

items.q: Which letter shows 1 12?
items.e: Each whole is split into 4 equal parts, so each mark is 14. 1 12 = 1 24: go to 1, then 2 more marks. That is letter B.

items.q: Which letter shows 116?
items.e: Each whole is split into 6 equal parts, so each mark is 16. 116 = 1 56: go to 1, then 5 more marks. That is letter A.

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed numeral.
items.e: Each whole is split into 6 equal parts, so each mark is 16. The arrow is 1 mark after 2. So it shows 2 16 = 136.

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is split into 5 equal parts, so each mark is 15. The arrow is 1 mark after 2. So it shows 2 15 = 115. Count all the marks from 0: 11.

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed numeral.
items.e: Each whole is split into 3 equal parts, so each mark is 13. The arrow is 2 marks after 2. So it shows 2 23 = 83.

items.q: Which fraction is between 12 and 34?
items.e: In eighths: 12 = 48 and 34 = 68. 58 is between them. 78 and 45 are more than 34, and 38 is less than 12.

items.q: Which number is between 2 14 and 2 34?
items.e: In eighths: 2 14 = 188 and 2 34 = 228. 198 is between them. 178 is too small, 238 is too big, and 94 is equal to 2 14, not between.

items.q: Which fraction is closest to 1?
items.e: Use sixteenths: 916, 78 = 1416, 34 = 1216, 58 = 1016. The one nearest to 1616 is 1416, so 78 is closest to 1. Big numbers in a fraction do not make it close to 1.

items.q: Mia eats 38 of a pizza. Lachlan eats 12 of a pizza of the same size. Who eats more?
items.e: Use eighths: 12 = 48. 4 eighths is more than 3 eighths, so Lachlan eats more.

items.q: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Jack eats 34 of it. How many slices does he eat?
items.e: 4 × 2 = 8, so 34 = 68. Jack eats 6 slices.

items.q: At the athletics carnival, Oliver runs 2 34 km and Isla runs 2 58 km. Who runs further?
items.e: Both ran 2 whole kilometres, so compare 34 and 58. 34 = 68, which is more than 58. So Oliver runs further.

items.q: In class 5M, 25 of the students play netball. In class 5K, 310 of the students play netball. Which class has the greater fraction of netball players?
items.e: Use tenths: 25 = 410. 4 tenths is more than 3 tenths, so 5M has the greater fraction. A bigger denominator does not mean a bigger fraction.

items.q: Ava says 25 of her class and 410 of her class are the same number of students. Is she right?
c: No. 410 is more
You can’t tell without the class size
Yes. 25 = 410
No. 25 is more
items.e: Multiply the numerator and the denominator of 25 by 2: 25 = 410. They are equivalent fractions, so they are the same number of students. Yes, she is right.

items.q: A koala can sleep for about 56 of a day. A wombat can sleep for about 23 of a day. Which animal sleeps for the greater part of the day?
items.e: Use sixths: 23 = 46. 5 sixths is more than 4 sixths, so the koala sleeps for longer.

items.q: For a sausage sizzle, each packet holds 6 sausages. The class cooks 19 sausages. How many packets is that, as a mixed numeral?
items.e: 6 sausages make 1 packet. 3 × 6 = 18, and 19 − 18 = 1 sausage is left. So 196 = 3 16 packets.

items.q: Four students measure their ribbons. Leo: 34 m. Chloe: 78 m. Kai: 58 m. Zara: 12 m. Who has the longest ribbon?
items.e: Use eighths: 34 = 68, 78, 58, 12 = 48. The longest is Chloe’s ribbon.

items.q: Noah says, “18 is greater than 14, because 8 is greater than 4.” Is he right?
c: No. 18 is less than 14
Yes. Eighths are bigger than quarters
items.e: A bigger denominator means the whole is cut into more, smaller parts. 14 = 28, which is more than 18. So 18 is less than 14.

items.q: Ruby says 2 35 = 65. What is the correct improper fraction?
items.e: Ruby multiplied 2 × 3. Instead, 2 wholes = 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add 3 fifths: 10 + 3 = 13. So 2 35 = 135.

items.q: At sport, Liam drinks 710 L of water and Sienna drinks 35 L. Who drinks more?
items.e: Use tenths: 35 = 610. 7 tenths is more than 6 tenths, so Liam drinks more.

items.q: In the long jump, Harper jumps 2 34 m, Cooper jumps 2 58 m and Mei jumps 2 12 m. Order them from the longest jump to the shortest.
items.e: All jumped 2 whole metres, so compare the fractions in eighths: 34 = 68, 58, 12 = 48. So the order is Harper, Cooper, Mei.

items.q: A tray of lamingtons is cut into 12 equal pieces. Kai’s family eats 9 pieces. Which fraction is equal to the part they eat?
items.e: 9 out of 12 pieces = 912. Divide the numerator and the denominator by 3: 912 = 34. 14 is the part that is left.

items.q: Grace walks 114 km to the beach. Write this distance as a mixed numeral.
items.e: 4 × 2 = 8 and 11 − 8 = 3. So 114 km = 2 34 km.

items.q: Three classes each have the same size tin of paint. Class 5A uses 34 of theirs, class 5B uses 916 and class 5C uses 58. Which class uses the least paint?
items.e: Use sixteenths: 34 = 1216, 916, 58 = 1016. The smallest is 916, so class 5B uses the least. 16 is the biggest denominator, but that does not make it the biggest fraction.

items.q: At footy training, Ethan runs 7 laps. Each lap is 14 km. That is 74 km. Is it more or less than 2 km?
c: Less. 74 km = 1 34 km
More. 74 km = 7 14 km
items.e: 4 quarters make 1 km and 8 quarters make 2 km. 7 quarters is 1 quarter short of 2 km, so 74 km = 1 34 km, which is less than 2 km.

items.q: Aarav has read 712 of his book. Matilda has read 23 of the same book. Who has read more?
items.e: Use twelfths: 23 = 812. 8 twelfths is more than 7 twelfths, so Matilda has read more.

items.q: Classes 5W and 5T each have 24 students. 34 of 5W and 58 of 5T go on the school excursion. How many more students from 5W go?
items.e: 34 = 68, which is 2 eighths more than 58. One eighth of 24 is 24 ÷ 8 = 3. 5W: 18 students (34 of 24). 5T: 15 students. 18 − 15 = 3 students.

items.q: A recipe needs 54 cups of flour. Charlotte has 1 12 cups. Does she have enough?
c: No. 1 12 = 24, which is less than 54
No. 1 12 = 34, which is less than 54
Yes. 1 12 = 64, which is more than 54
items.e: Write 1 12 in quarters: 1 whole = 44 and 12 = 24, so 1 12 = 64. 64 > 54, so yes, she has enough.

items.q: Two families drive the same road to Adelaide. Amelia’s family has driven 56 of the way. William’s family has driven 23 of the way. Who is closer to Adelaide?
c: They are the same distance away
items.e: Use sixths: 23 = 46. Amelia’s family has driven 5 sixths, so only 1 sixth is left. William’s family has 2 sixths left. Amelia’s family is closer.
